faqs.q: An opossum keeps getting under my Belton house. Is that a problem?

Belton.wildlife_intro:
Belton keeps our crew busy around the Saluda River side of town and its older mill housing. Two problems account for most visits: groundhogs burrowing at field and foundation edges, and skunks under porches.

Older frame homes near the center, brick ranches from the postwar decades, and farmhouses along the county roads each bring different attic and crawlspace problems. Cooler Upstate winters create a hard fall deadline: animals that find attic warmth in October stay until spring, so sealing work done before the first cold snap matters more here than on the coast.

Removal without repair does not hold in Belton, so our visits pair the animal work with sealing and screening sized to the house itself.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Honea Path home?
faqs.a: Bat work here is exclusion only, and no permit is required to remove bats in South Carolina. What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my Honea Path lawn at night and it smells like skunk. What is going on?
faqs.a: That combination is a striped skunk hunting grubs — the small cone-shaped holes across a lawn are its signature — and a den under a porch, deck, or crawlspace edge is usually nearby. Skunks are South Carolina's number-two rabies carrier in Department of Public Health testing, and routine relocation is against state law, so our crew traps calmly at the den with covered traps, handles the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and screens the den opening so the next skunk finds it closed.

faqs.a: Yes — nine-banded armadillos are established throughout the entirety of South Carolina, and Iva is no exception. They root up lawns hunting grubs and worms and dig burrows under porches, driveways, and crawlspace edges near Lake Hartwell and Russell Lake creek arms in the county's south. We trap the animals working your property and then backfill and screen the burrow openings, because an open burrow is quickly claimed by the next armadillo — or by a skunk or opossum. Our Iva crew traces it by inspection instead of demolition, removes and sanitizes, and closes the access that let the animal in. If the dead animal is a raccoon, skunk, fox, or bat, we handle it with rabies precautions and can advise on Department of Public Health testing when there was pet or human exposure.

Iva.wildlife_intro:
What makes Iva different from the next town over is the Lake Hartwell and Russell Lake creek arms in the county's south. More than anything else, we are called for raccoons in older mill-village attics and gray squirrels in hardwood canopy.

Housing here mixes college and mill-era streets with lake and farm properties at the edges, much of it shaded by mature hardwood canopy. Foothill ground means wooded slopes behind the houses: groundhogs hold burrows on the banks, skunks work the lawn edges, and squirrels drop from hardwood limbs straight onto roofs.

The last step on a Iva call is a walk-around with the homeowner: each entry we sealed, each burrow we screened, and what to watch for when the seasons turn.
